book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See
essays: A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World
Spirituality Similar Ways of Seeing the World
“I knew I’d know it when I knew it” (King Bumi, “Sozin's Comet, Part 2 The Old Masters”)
The Proud Disabled Person as Counterstory
Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within
samples: Aaron Ehasz, ATLA's head writer, reflects that the show tested its characters' belief systems against their humanity: Aang's attempt to comfort himself with Buddhist detachment fails when Appa is taken, and he cannot let go of his love for Katara to unblock his final chakra and enter the Avatar State. Yet Uncle Iroh shows the opposite lesson, since by studying Water Tribe ideas he invents lightning redirection, the technique that lets Zuko survive his father and lets Team Avatar save the world. The preface concludes that philosophy both limits and unlocks human potential, capped with a joke about Hegel and hard ice cream.

De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.

Belarde-Lewis (Zuni/Tlingit) and Bordeaux (Lakota) read ATLA through Indigenous philosophy: V.F. Cordova's 'bounded space' explains how each nation's landscape shapes its people and benders, with Tui and La, the badgermoles, flying bison, and dragons as other-than-human teachers, and Shawn Wilson's relationality frames Yue's sacrifice, the Lion Turtle's elder wisdom, and the Order of the White Lotus as intergenerational balance rather than power. Aang's energybending of Ozai ('Sozin's Comet') shows that balance across generations matters more than power over the world, and the Lion Turtle makes the universe '(Lion) Turtles all the way down'.

Ortiz-Hinojosa asks what is most fundamental in ATLA's world, testing Toph's metalbending, lava- and sandbending, energybending, and the Spirit World against Empedocles' four roots, Anaximander's undifferentiated apeiron, Heraclitus's fire and flux, the Nahua teotl, and Chinese qi and Hindu prana. She concludes that energy is plausibly the fundamental basis from which the four Elements differentiate, making the deepest reality of ATLA a non-physical interdependence, while stressing that even Guru Pathik and the past Avatars lack complete knowledge of their own universe, just as we do.

Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.

Whittaker argues ATLA is an abolitionist text about nationhood itself: the show first naturalizes the four nations through the four elements, so that Hama and Zuko are expelled from their host communities the moment their bending is revealed ('The Puppetmaster', 'Zuko Alone'), much as Beauvoir showed gender is naturalized from sex. It then denaturalizes both through Huu's swamp unity, Iroh bending fire like water ('Bitter Work'), and Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation'. Drawing on Black abolitionism and Denise Ferreira da Silva's 'difference without separability', he concludes Aang's task is not to save a world of nations but to make the world like him.

book: 141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko
essays: A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World
Spirituality Similar Ways of Seeing the World
“I knew I’d know it when I knew it” (King Bumi, “Sozin's Comet, Part 2 The Old Masters”)
The Proud Disabled Person as Counterstory
Every Soul Experiences the Battle Within
samples: Head writer Aaron Ehasz asks what philosophy is for in ATLA and answers with the writers' unconscious conclusion: characters' belief systems are always tested against their humanity, and Aang's Buddhist detachment fails him twice, once when he loses Appa and once when opening the final chakra demands he let go of Katara. The counterexample is Iroh, whose study of Water Tribe techniques lets a firebender invent lightning redirection, the skill that lets Zuko survive his father and lets the saga resolve. So philosophy is not crushed by human need but is the key that unlocks humanity's potential, provided we stay open to ideas from other cultures.

The editors argue ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang learns slowly and non-linearly, needs a teacher for each element, stays weaker than Katara or Toph in specific skills, and saving the world is a team effort in which he is neither leader nor brains. They identify the show's unifying theme as oneness, the 'illusion of separation' voiced by Guru Pathik and the swampbender Huu, and trace it to East and South Asian schools such as Huayan and Chan Buddhism and to Indigenous traditions. Philosophy is presented as the tool the show itself uses against genocide, imperialism, and ecological destruction, with Ba Sing Se's 'no war' denial as the cautionary case.

Two Indigenous scholars read the whole bending world through V.F. Cordova's 'bounded space' and Shawn Wilson's relationality: each nation's bending flows from responsible relationship to its landscape, animals, and spirits, as when waterbending comes from observing Tui and La, or Toph and Aang learn earthbending and airbending from badgermoles and sky bison, flattening the human-animal hierarchy. Yue's sacrifice to become the Moon Spirit is read alongside Tlingit clan insignia earned by ancestral self-gift. The Lion Turtle's teaching that bending began as bending one's own energy, and the Order of the White Lotus restoring Ba Sing Se, show that balance is an intergenerational responsibility rather than power over others.

A metaphysics chapter asks how many fundamental substances the ATLA world contains, starting from Toph's metalbending, sandbending, and the Lion Turtle's energybending as anomalies for the four-Element doctrine. It tests the system against Empedocles' four roots moved by Love and Strife, Anaximander's undifferentiated apeiron, Heraclitus' fire and flux, and the Nahua teotl of James Maffie, also weighing qi, chakras, and the Spirit World for monism versus dualism. The favored conclusion is that energy is a semi-incorporeal life force underlying the Elements, so the deepest reality of ATLA is non-physical interdependence, and the heroes' uncertainty mirrors our own unfinished physics.

A martial artist maps each bending style onto the real art it animates and its parent philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies wu-wei, shown when she spares Yon Rha in 'The Southern Raiders' as strength rather than weakness; Toph's Hong Jia earthbending grounds her insistence on truth, an example of the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech; Zuko's driven Northern Shaolin temperament walks through the first three Noble Truths, from suffering caused by desire for his honor to its cessation when he joins Team Avatar; and Aang's Baguazhang airbending expresses freedom as openness to change and to Iroh's counsel. The Avatar's power is therefore not four bendings but the combination of the four character strengths.

Whittaker argues the show's real target is nationhood itself: the four nations look natural because benders seem born to one element, so Zuko is expelled from an Earth Kingdom village in 'Zuko Alone' and Hama can never count as Fire Nation. Against this, Huu's 'one big living organism' swamp, Iroh bending fire like water to redirect lightning, and Guru Pathik's lesson that even the separation of the four elements is an illusion denaturalize the elements and with them the nations. Borrowing Beauvoir's point that gender social systems masquerade as natural sex, and Denise Ferreira da Silva's 'difference without separability,' the chapter reads ATLA as an abolitionist text: Aang's task is not to save a world of nations but to make the world like him.

book: 142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers
essays: Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers
Maybe Jen’s Reading this Chapter Right Now
Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals
“This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”
Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of
Appendix Why are there Four Volumes of Avengers
samples: Editor Mark D. White introduces the volume: the Avengers fascinate because they are equal parts superhero epic and soap opera, and the contributors' questions mirror that mix. He previews the book's guiding questions—whether Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor embody three different moral philosophies, whether the Kree-Skrull War bears on the ethics of war, why the team keeps admitting reformed criminals like Hawkeye, Quicksilver, and the Scarlet Witch, whether Kang can kill his past self, whether we secretly admire Norman Osborn's Dark Avengers, and whether the android Vision can truly love the Scarlet Witch. It frames the collection but applies no philosophical framework itself.

White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.

Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.

Southworth and Tallman ask why fans blame Hank Pym for Ultron's killings while never crediting Magneto for fathering two heroes, and answer with Aristotle's account of character formed by habitual imitation, renewed as 'moral exemplarism': praise and blame track exemplarship, not biology. Scott Lang earned credit because he actively taught Cassie right and wrong, making her the hero Stature; T'Chaka and stepmother Ramonda shaped T'Challa, while Heinrich Zemo's Nazi upbringing warped Helmut into the new Baron Zemo. The Avengers themselves—Cap's patient mentoring of Hawkeye, Stark hiring ex-con Scott Lang—function as moral exemplars for reformed villains, so the mentoring 'parents', not the siring ones, deserve the credit or blame.

Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.

Cook analyzes John Byrne's and Dan Slott's She-Hulk runs as metacomics: Jen breaks the fourth wall to threaten readers into buying her book, deduces how long she was unconscious from comic-book time, steps across the gutter between panels to travel, and even attacks her own creator. Weezie's line 'We're inked and colored! Printed!' raises the problem that once published, the characters' actions are fixed, while her backstory (staying in print to stop aging) exploits comic conventions. The chapter ends by asking whether the Official Handbook's conflicting retcons make Jen's meta-awareness a delusion or a superpower, and what that uncertainty means for truth in metafiction and our understanding of comics storytelling itself.

book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul
essays: All Joking Aside, This Is a Modal Muddle
What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum
Leaving the Shadow of the Bat
samples: Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.

James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'

Stephen Kershnar argues that Batman's hatred of criminals is not a vice but a virtue, since hating what is evil is the morally appropriate attitude toward wrongdoers like the Joker or Batman: Year One's brutal Detective Flass. Against Aristotle's person-focused Virtuous-Persons Theory he defends a 'Virtuous-Thoughts-and-Actions Theory,' illustrated by Gordon's retaliatory beating of Flass and Batman elbow-smashing a pimp in Year One. The chapter closes on the golden mean of balanced love and hate: Batman's virtuous hatred leaves his life isolated and unflourishing, showing that virtue does not guarantee eudaimonia.

Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.

Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.

Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.

book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There
essays: “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”
This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again
Who They Are or Who They Want to Be
It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life
samples: Show writer David Weddle recounts how Ronald Moore pushed the 'Act of Contrition' script beyond Star Trek-style expository dialogue into interleaved flashback snippets dramatizing Starbuck's guilt over passing Zak Adama's flight test. He argues this stream-of-consciousness technique, letting memories, dreams and hallucinations flow out of characters' inner emotional lives (as later in 'Scar' and 'Maelstrom'), is what made the series groundbreaking, echoing Faulkner's 'the past isn't over. It isn't even past.' The foreword frames the book's philosophical interest as rooted in the show's narrative form itself.

The introduction argues, via Edward James Olmos's campus talks, that Battlestar Galactica is 'truth' television that dares viewers to think about war, insurgency, torture, abortion, genocide, race and identity. It traces the franchise from Glen Larson's 1978 original through Galactica 1980 to the Moore/Eick re-imagining, insisting the show is 'a cultural discussion' rather than a cultural artifact. Borrowing Orson Scott Card's claim that real science fiction works like true religious literature, it frames the contributors' essays as probing who we are, our place in the universe, and how we find or make meaning, and explains the book's conventions for naming the Sixes, Eights, Sharons and its own anonymous 'Final Five' chapters.

Milsky applies the narrative theory of personal identity drawn from Paul Ricoeur and Alasdair MacIntyre (we are the story we emplot about ourselves) to the two Sharons: Boomer's discovery that she is a sleeper Cylon is a 'factual disruption' of her self-story (she shoots Adama because her human narrative cannot cohere), while Athena's love for Helo is a 'disruption of belief' that rewrites her values about humans. He extends the analysis to humans: Starbuck's repressed childhood abuse, Roslin's Pythian-prophecy conversion, and Helo's love for a Cylon, plus Six expelling Athena and Tyrol refusing to acknowledge Boomer, show identity is also socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy. The chapter concludes disruptions are not identity-altering: like the Final Five in 'Crossroads, Part 2' (Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh, I am an officer in the Colonial Fleet'), integration and retelling preserve the continuity of self.

Booth argues the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across media, so viewers must actively construct the story (which is why Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' only makes sense if you watched them), and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performative roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's wet-floor amnesia in 'Water,' and Hera's human-Cylon hybridity as postmodern identity-in-process. Against Baltar, who waits for D'Anna to assign him an identity, Tigh actively constructs his ('that's the man I want to be'), and the chapter ends suggesting viewers too become human-machine hybrids by constructing themselves from the show's fragments.

Cuddy argues the gamer's bond with the avatar is an extension of the ego: Freud's id/ego/superego model explains why playing a Cylon Raider or flying the 'Bastille Day' mission lets gamers reconcile unconscious desires with the superego's demands in ways reality forbids. But when we lose we disconnect from the avatar and blame the game or 'cheating' opponents, which Sartre diagnoses as bad faith, a denial of freedom, contrasted with Adama's 'a man takes responsibility for his actions' in '33' and Baltar's vacillation over the vice-presidency. Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.

The chapter reads Baltar's head-Six and Caprica Six's head-Baltar through the gothic Double and Doppelganger tradition and Dissociative Identity Disorder: Number Six is Baltar's repressed guilt over betraying humanity ('I'm your subconscious frakking with your mind'), letting him escape responsibility for signing execution orders in 'Precipice,' while Gina Six serves as a tangible Double. Plato's Symposium myth of the split self frames Baltar and Six as two halves of one whole, since he cannot function without some version of Six present, physical or hallucinated. The resolution is Aristotle's golden mean from Book Two of the Nicomachean Ethics: like integration therapy for DID, virtue is a balance between extremes rather than eliminating one side, so Baltar and Six's child Hera may embody the balanced union of human and Cylon.

samples: Dean Kowalski's introduction pitches the volume: philosophy's big questions about what is really real, how we ought to behave, and what we can know brought to Sheldon's spot on the couch. It previews the essays to come — Aristotle weighing Sheldon's way of life, Hobbes applauding the roommate agreement, Kant deriding 'un-unravelable webs' of lies — and frames the book's running thought that comic-book and sci-fi geekery can be put to serious philosophical use, while even Sheldon cannot escape the 'inexplicable need for human contact.'

Greg Littmann tests Sheldon's geek existence against Aristotle's ideal of living well: since humanity's distinctive function is reason (the DVD-player-and-screwdriver argument), a life devoted to thought like Sheldon's — down to his fantasy of being a thinking satellite in orbit — has genuine Aristotelian worth. The chapter argues Aristotle could even bless geek obsessions, because poetry explores universal hypotheticals (Terminator causal loops, Superman's laundry) and adventure fiction purges emotion much as tragedy's catharsis does. But Sheldon's arrogance ('Captain Arrogant'), rigid clinging to his spot on the couch, and selfishness toward Leonard and Howard would earn failing marks in virtue, so the modern geek gets a mixed yet partly vindicating report card.

Kowalski maps Aristotle's three kinds of friendship onto the gang: pleasure-friendships (Halo and paintball nights, and Raj's fury when Howard abandons their kite fight for a jogger), utility-friendships (Sheldon's failed Friendship Algorithm bid on Kripke for lab access, and the roommate agreement's Friendship Rider invoked over the CERN trip). Complete friendship — mutual care for the other's own sake between moral equals — looks closest in Leonard and Sheldon, yet Sheldon's pancake-breakfast apology collapses the moment Leonard refuses to take him to Switzerland ('Drat. No Frodo for you'), exposing contractual utility where genuine care should be. The chapter concludes no pairing in the show achieves Aristotle's rare complete friendship, and asks whether similarity is really required for true 'besties.'

Sayles sorts the show's technology use by Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: healthy supplements (Raj webcamming his parents in India, Sheldon and Amy's video dates) versus unhealthy substitutes (Penny's Age of Conan spiral into unwashed hair and sick days, Sheldon living as a 'mobile virtual presence device,' one-sided 'virtual vengeance' videos against Penny's Wi-Fi theft and Kripke's helium prank). Since the mean is relative to the person and situation rather than a mathematical midpoint, moderation must be found case by case, and man as a social being must keep his social skills exercised. The chapter finds Penny and Amy — not the four scientists — best model balanced technology use.

Clifton asks whether fans are moral monsters for laughing at behavior that looks autistic, running Sheldon through the DSM criteria for Asperger's syndrome: missing Penny's sarcasm about doctors who 'remove shoes from asses,' hedging the bath-item Christmas gift, and inflexibly clinging to nonfunctional routines like Saturday-night laundry. Setting the writers' stated intentions aside as one fallible piece of evidence (the intentional-fallacy debate), he weighs the medical model of disability (leveling and normalizing) against the social-constructivist model in which disability is a misfit between trait and environment. Because Sheldon has built a world — theoretical physics, accommodating friends, the comic book store — where his traits are advantages, even an 'alpha nerd' leader, they constitute an 'enability' rather than a disability, and the laughter is morally innocent.

Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.

book: 146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom
samples: Editor Peter Fosl's introduction argues that a box-office-disappointment stoner comedy is genuinely philosophical: the film confronts sex, violence, and death (Donny dies, Maude conceives, marmots are drowned), stages class war between the unemployed Dude and the capitalist 'achiever' Big Lebowski, and sets the Dude's pacifist abiding against Walter's Vietnam warrior ethic and European nihilism. People are drawn to the Dude as an exemplar of stoic, nonmaterialistic abiding, and the essays draw on thinkers from Aristotle and Epicurus to Derrida and Butler; Ethan Coen's Princeton philosophy thesis on Wittgenstein anchors the film's pedigree.

Zeccardi and Ma deconstruct the film's hierarchical dichotomy between Walter's rule-obsessed ethical generalism (Shabbas rules, 'MARK IT ZERO!') and the nihilists' particularist 'Zere ARE no ROOLZ', using Derrida and Culler's method of undermining the opposition the text privileges. Each extreme fails: Walter's principles collide in the beeper dilemma, and active Nietzschean nihilism makes the nihilists unpredictable cowards. The Dude emerges as an Aristotelian agent of virtue whose phronesis perceptively weighs contextual facts (Smokey's disputed toe, the carpet-pissers' false assumption) against principles, making 'What would the Dude do?' a question about character rather than rules.

Jackson models the Dude as a formal system whose axioms are bowling, White Russians, and the rug, so that the counterexample to 'Jeffrey Lebowski = Jeffrey Lebowski' precipitates a foundational crisis just as Russell's paradox shattered Frege's set theory and non-Euclidean geometry unsettled Euclid's fifth postulate. Gödel's incompleteness theorems then show the Dude's system was never complete: no matter how many axioms (rugs) he regains, true-but-unprovable statements remain. His final reply is to adopt 'the Dude abides' as a new self-referential axiom asserting its own consistency — which, by Gödel's second theorem, a consistent system cannot do; hence 'fuck it, let's go bowling'.

Eberl asks whether the Dude's 'pure abiding' is happiness: he runs Bentham's utility calculus on Dude-style pleasures (bowling's fecundity, the rug's purity, attending Marty's dance quintet for long-term rent goodwill) and Mill's higher/lower pleasures (Maude's vaginal art versus Logjammin'). Aristotle's verdict is that the Dude is not flourishing — his pleasures are incomplete, losable (the burned Torino), and he neglects his rational, social nature — yet Aristotle also ranks friendship with Walter and Donny highly, and Pieper's leisure, built on Aquinas's contemplation, gives the Dude's leisure a partial defense: he is incomplete but not bad, and he 'lives' while achievers merely make a living.

O'Loughlin reads Walter biting off a nihilist's ear and the Dude refusing to walk out on league play as concrete realizations of ancient friendship: Aristotle's eudaimonia requires friends as 'second selves' whose shared activity (bowling in the friends' company) structures the excellent life, while Epicurus's Garden ordered life around simple pleasures and ataraxia, with friendship supplying pleasant memory and a kind of immortality after death. Because we moderns claim friendship's value without practicing its costs, the Dude's priorities look comic yet pierce us — and Donny's death, the Ralph's coffee can, and 'let's go bowling' become Epicurean commemoration rather than irreverence.

Rempel argues the Dude is a modern Epicurean parable: Epicurus's ataraxia is freedom from disturbance achieved by limiting desires to the natural and necessary — simple food, shelter, a few friends — so the Dude's 69-cent check, whale-song baths, and contentment with four dollars ('almost five') express 'enough is enough'. Maude's easily-had, non-binding seduction fits Epicurus's classification of sex as natural but not necessary (Lucretius: choose the joys of Venus without penalty), while Walter's million-dollar ringer scheme and his 'sick Cynthia thing' personify vain, insatiable desires — 'contented poverty is an honorable estate', so the Dude may be the wealthiest man in Los Angeles County.

book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book
essays: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the ADAM
“Your Flesh, Too, is Weak. But You Have… Potential”
The Plurality of Worlds to Come
Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow
samples: Luke Cuddy's introduction tours the philosophical riches of the Shock series: the Little Sister's idealized vision of Rapture in BioShock 2, Andrew Ryan as a male counterpart of Ayn Rand, the Motorized Patriots of Columbia, SHODAN's god complex, Elizabeth's tears, and Comstock's prophecy. It frames the volume's guiding questions, such as whether BioShock legitimately critiques Rand's philosophy and whether Booker ever had free will, and closes by invoking the 'false philosopher' mark (knowledge without justification) before inviting the reader to turn the page.

Pointon argues the 'would you kindly' twist in Andrew Ryan's office works on two levels at once: it reveals Jack's conditioning within the game and simultaneously falsifies the player's meta-narrative of playing a free agent. He uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to explain why games literally extend cognition and body (mirror-neuron empathy with Little Sisters, craning your neck while peeking around corners), and Gadamer's hermeneutic horizons and fusion of horizons to explain how BioShock deliberately builds and then shatters player expectations. The three alternative endings keyed to saving or harvesting Little Sisters then restore a third horizon in which the player, like Jack fighting Fontaine, is a 'man' who chooses rather than a slave who obeys, a critique of linear RPGs that only feign autonomy.

Rose argues BioShock is not a cheap strawman of Ayn Rand but a use of her own philosophy-through-fiction method (Atlas Shrugged as the hidden utopia Rapture continues) to show what happens when an ideologue divides reason from emotion. Ryan, unlike the flawless John Galt, is a flawed human destroyed by his refusal to question and by sentiment (killed by the son he cannot shoot), while Fontaine wins by manipulating feelings and Tenenbaum's motherly attachment to the Little Sisters becomes her salvation. Drawing on Antonio Damasio's point that emotion filters options for practical reasoning, the chapter reads the save-or-harvest dilemma as proof that moral choices must include emotional response, concluding Randians should celebrate a game that warns against being blinded by ideology rather than against Objectivism itself.

Mentyka maps the two antagonists of System Shock 2 onto the two classical criteria of personal identity: the parasitic Many, one flesh persisting through wildly different bodies, embody the bodily criterion, while the rogue AI SHODAN, pure data abandoning first Citadel then the Von Braun, embodies psychological continuity from Locke's memory theory. He runs the standard objections (Reid and Butler on memory's circularity, cell replacement, cybernetic implants, sleep and infancy) against both sides, then turns to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, only relations of degree, likening the reused 'Soldier #G65434-2' avatar to a person surviving through successors. The player character, physical like the Many yet armed with SHODAN's cybernetic knowledge, suggests identity needs both body and mind.

Origitano reads Elizabeth through Beauvoir and Frye: Columbia's propaganda infantilizes and objectifies her ('the Seed of the Prophet', 'Lamb', 'Specimen', always defined relative to a man), the tower literalizes Frye's birdcage of systematic oppression, and her confinement for an uncontrollable power mirrors women caged by a supposed natural inferiority. Booker's rescue only grants freedom, echoing Beauvoir's point that women have 'only received' what men are willing to give, so Elizabeth remains caged as his poker chip, her lock-picking skills formed by captivity and her tears dismissed as foreign. Her emancipation comes through action and collective solidarity, allying with Lady Comstock's ghost, taking control of Songbird, and finally drowning Booker/Comstock as equals, which enacts Beauvoir's claim that liberation must be won, not granted.

Cook asks whether Rapture's Plasmids and ghosts refute physicalism and answers no: Plasmid powers are genetically engineered via ADAM and thus describable in physical vocabulary, while contractor Bill McDonagh's audio diary explains the ghosts of Rapture as leaked memories passed through gene-swapping, so all their facts supervene on physical facts in Chalmers's sense. The classic anti-physicalist pressures, Chalmers's zombie argument and the Nagel-style gap between objective physical description and subjective qualia ('the smell of poo'), do not apply because Rapture's phenomena carry no extra subjective residue. Invoking Clarke's third law that advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, he concludes Andrew Ryan did not choose the impossible.

book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections
essays: Our First Gaze into the Black Mirror
The Grain Can Lead Us to Know Too Much
A White Christmas with Dark Reflections
A Black Mirror of Our Anxieties
Forget Cooper. Are We in a Simulation
Do We Attain Justice by Punishment
What Not to Do as a Parent
Two Philosophies, Two Compasses to Navigate Life
samples: The book's introduction argues that Black Mirror does philosophy the way Sartre's No Exit and earlier philosophical fictions (Lucian, Ibn al-Nafis, More, Bacon, Defoe) do: its near-future scenarios — the pig spectacle of The National Anthem, Nosedive's star ratings — work as thought experiments and social criticism rather than simple 'warnings about technology,' since Brooker insists the show is about the human condition, not gadgets. It applies Wittgenstein's duck–rabbit 'seeing as' distinction to explain why two viewers of the same episode may legitimately see different philosophical arguments in it, which is exactly what the book's chapters then do. It closes by presenting each episode (and each chapter) as a self-contained philosophical prompt.

Collins and Boesch use Prime Minister Callow's coerced live sex act with a pig in The National Anthem to weigh conflicting moral obligations: the public's initial 72% Kantian refusal flips to an 86% utilitarian capitulation after the kidnapper's finger video, and the withheld revelation that Susannah was released half an hour early undermines any consequentialist justification of the act. A virtue-theory reading faults Callow's character for faking the rescue video and putting self-interest first, and the UKN media's Kantian compliance collapses once ratings are at stake. The closing section applies Martha Nussbaum's theory of disgust (contamination transferring disgust from blood and vomit to the spectacle-watchers themselves) to argue the episode's graphic imagery functions as a moral emotion condemning the audience's own obsession with spectacle.

Reading Fifteen Million Merits through Marx, the chapter treats Bing's world of endless pedaling, Wraith Babes, and Hot Shot as a commodity society in which people themselves carry use and exchange values — Oliver the 'lemon,' Glee deemed 'quite worthless,' Abi's unsellable papier-mache penguin discarded as detritus. Marx's commodity fetish explains the universalized pricing in merits, and Lukacs-style reification shows things commanding people (Cuppliance compelling compliance). Adorno's culture industry explains why all the shows share one form and why Bing's glass-shard rebellion is absorbed as just another commodity, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man supplies the hope that reason, love (Bing's love for Abi as something 'real'), and switching off the media can still seed resistance.

The chapter argues that the Grain in The Entire History of You ruins Liam and Ffion's marriage not because the truth is bad but because total transparency destroys trust (via Luhmann), feeds a paranoid cycle where any deleted footage looks like guilt, and strips Fi of authority over her own life story. Goffman, Plessner, and Simmel ground the claim that social masks, tact, and privacy are preconditions of selfhood, while Sartre's 'look' explains Fi's shame when Liam forces her to replay her infidelity and Rousseau explains how dependence on others' gaze makes us unfree. Framed by Foucault's reading of Oedipus as a victim of his own knowledge, it concludes that Liam should have let the past lie — and ends with Byung-Chul Han's transparency society as our own already-arrived trajectory.

Against the natural reading that Be Right Back fails because AshBot is a poor copy, the chapter argues that even a perfect duplicate, AshBot+, would not be Ash: like a perfect forgery of a twenty-dollar bill, it would share all intrinsic but none of Ash's relational properties (being Martha's beloved, the coming father of her child), which also exposes a fission paradox for psychological-continuity theories. Nozick's account of love as a 'we' — shared memory, autonomy, and well-being — explains why Martha cannot trade up or replace a dead partner without destroying the self constituted by the relationship. Parfit's view that only psychological continuity matters is then rejected: because Martha's relationship survives only if Ash does, survival itself matters, and Martha must mourn rather than cling to a specter.

The chapter tests the White Bear Justice Park's daily torture of Victoria Skillane against every major theory of punishment: Kant and Hegel's retributivism makes her deserve punishment (her crime could not be universalized and annulled justice) but cannot justify a punishment disproportionate to the crime. Locke's memory criterion suggests Punished Victoria is not the person who did the crime, though Parfit's psychological continuity and Thomson's bodily continuity restore the identity. Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism partially vindicates the park as deterrence and incapacitation, but cannot explain the laughing crowds — which Machiavelli's civic spectacle and Nietzsche's genealogy of punishment (Schadenfreude as moralized creditor-debtor pleasure) explain: the crowd is gleefully reenacting Victoria's own crime and calling it justice.

samples: The editors frame the volume: Stan Lee and Jack Kirby created the first Black superhero in Fantastic Four no. 52 (1966) during the Civil Rights era, when an advanced African nation or a Black president seemed unthinkable to many Americans, and Stan's 1968 'Stan's Soapbox' column called for destroying bigotry by exposing it rather than punching it. They present Wakanda as significant but imperfect, and position the contributors' philosophical essays on racism, colonialism, feminism, spirituality, and Afrofuturism as continuing Lee and Kirby's tradition, with Coogler's 'one single tribe' message as the through-line.

Boudreaux reads Wakanda's Challenge Day and Killmonger's coup through Edmund Burke's critique of the French Revolution, arguing that pure reason divorced from tradition cannot supply social cohesion: M'Baku's reverence for the ritual combat allows a peaceful transfer of power, and the ceremony itself checks arbitrary rule by making T'Challa fight stripped of Panther powers. Killmonger's disregard for custom ('Weeks? I don't need weeks') and burning of the Heart-Shaped Herb garden show revolution destroying what it claims to save, splitting Okoye's throne-loyalty against Nakia's 'I save my country,' while M'Baku sheltering T'Challa and T'Challa's incremental outreach centers embody the organic, gradual reform Burke endorsed over rationally designed reinvention.

Bein and Lewis imagine Killmonger surviving his duel to face Wakandan justice, and sort what justice would demand into retributive justice (Kant: punishment only what the offender deserves, never using him merely as a means to public safety, though they note Kant's own racist views), reparatory justice (Locke's natural rights and what Wakanda owes N'Jadaka for T'Chaka killing N'Jobu and abandoning him in Oakland), and the restorative-to-transformative justice of Changamire's gatherings in Coates's 'A Nation Under Our Feet,' modeled on South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. They argue a restorative Wakanda would seat Killmonger with his victims and even the king at the table to repair harm rather than imprison him, and sketch a prison-abolitionist Wakanda meeting Thanos with 'Wakandan justice is more civilized.'

Almassi contrasts Rawlsian ideal theory (the veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) with Charles Mills's critique that idealization marginalizes actual historic oppression, arguing the film's characters seek Aristotle's corrective justice in a world already steeped in wrongdoing: the 1991 deaths of W'Kabi's parents at Klaue's hands and of N'Jobu at T'Chaka's. He works through the Museum of Great Britain axe scene as restitution, W'Kabi's 'you kill him where he stands' and Killmonger's 'I'mma make sure we're even' as retribution (tested against Walen's proportionality principles, with vengeance untethered from legitimate punishment), and Nakia's and T'Challa's outreach centers as Margaret Urban Walker-style relational repair, reading T'Chaka's concealment of N'Jobu's death as actively constructed ignorance in service of isolationism.

Hobden argues Wakanda's isolationist 'us vs. them' politics is Western rather than African in spirit: Ramonda's branding of Killmonger as a 'charlatan' enacts Fricker's testimonial injustice and echoes the colonial epistemicide that dismissed African knowledge, while African philosophers (Etieyibo, Eze, Menkiti) derive cosmopolitan duties from ubuntu ('I am because we are') and Igbo proverbs like 'the right hand washes the left,' which welcome the stranger as a bearer of knowledge. She finds it striking that an isiXhosa-speaking Wakanda shows no trace of ubuntu, and reads T'Challa's UN speech as a Western-style aid relationship ('what would you like us to do about it?') rather than genuine recognition of shared humanity.

Graves sets T'Challa's liberal internationalism — UN sovereign equality and collective security, which he traces through the organization's Charter limits and its record of preserving the status quo — against Killmonger's Pan-Africanism, the liberation lineage of the 1900 Pan-African Conference, Du Bois's Pan-African Congresses, Garvey's UNIA, and Nkrumah's 'Africa Must Unite,' which N'Jobu and Killmonger carry forward with vibranium weapons after centuries of Wakandan indifference to slavery, colonialism, and apartheid. He argues collective security has repeatedly failed oppressed Black populations, making Killmonger's realist 'Africans must save themselves' position understandable, though he questions whether arms rather than aid can liberate and calls T'Challa's single Oakland outreach center inadequate to Wakanda's wealth.
